conclusion: Confirmed (small so far): v9 = 19.21 vs 20.10 us/layer (-4.4%), deterministic, 2.1e-4 rel err. Path: register prefetch spills; per-warp rings and split-K units drown in per-unit signalling (in-kernel phase timers: 36% atomics +fence tail, 14% publish, 20% compute); 16 x 512 B TMA row copies cap HBM at ~0.9 TB/s (fixed by repacking weights fragment-native, one bulk copy per unit; TMA-only delivery then 13.6 us = 82% of peak). Correctness bug found and fixed: WAR race between consumers' generic smem reads and the next TMA (async proxy) write into the same ring stage (compute-sanitizer racecheck) -> fence.proxy.async.shared::cta before releasing a stage. Robustness: bounded acquire waits + abort flag, no grid barrier, tiles in global order (no dependency cycles). Remaining gap to the 13.6 us delivery bound: ~5.6 us/layer.
hypothesis: A single persistent launch that prefetches weights across op boundaries beats back-to-back launches on the same bytes and can approach the read ceiling

conclusion: Not yet: best 44.42 vs 38.8 us/layer (+14%), numerically correct (2.9e-4 rel vs fp32, routing identical). Failures: splitting DOWN across CTAs (atomics + last-arriver) costs 5-15 us; >4 consumer warps or deeper rings do not help. Padding/self-reset bought ~3 us. Next: shrink router+route latency (both should be ~1-2 us).
hypothesis: Fusing router->route->expert GEMVs into one persistent launch removes launch gaps and lets routed-expert weights stream as soon as routing is known, beating the 4-launch path
title: Megakernel stage 2: whole MoE block (router, routing, grouped up, grouped down) in ONE persistent launch at M=5

conclusion: Not yet (44.48 vs 38.44 us/layer, +16%), but the kernel is now correct, deterministic and stall-free. Successes: route top-k 6.5x fewer cycles (bf16-exact logits -> u32 key, redux.sync.max; softmax denominator cancels in top-k renorm); deterministic group ids; dynamic ticket scheduler (-6 us vs static at the same config). Failures/corrections: (1) the earlier 36.9-37.2 us 'beats launches' result was a benchmark artifact - layers were independent, so layer l+1 overlapped layer l; with honest chaining it is 47.5. (2) Race found: warp-per-chunk consumers with STAGES % CW != 0 hit mbarrier parity aliasing (a warp passes try_wait.parity on a stale phase, reads stale weights, arrives early) -> sporadic wrong outputs at stages 5/6 and a producer stall; earlier stage-2 numbers at stages=6 (incl. 47.22) were from a racy config. (3) Harness use-after-free: op blob holds raw pointers; MoEProgram now keeps its inputs alive. Remaining critical path per layer: router ~8 us, route ~4 us, UP ~2 TB/s effective, DOWN ~9 us after the last UP tile.
hypothesis: Cutting the serial router->route latency and load-balancing expert tiles makes the single-launch MoE block beat the 4-launch path at M=5
title: Megakernel stage 2, round 2: MoE block in ONE persistent launch - route latency, honest chained timing, races, dynamic scheduling

conclusion: Partly: tensor-core streamed router cut 2.8 us (44.0 -> 41.23 us/layer) but the block is still +6.6% vs launches (38.7). Launch-path breakdown (router 4.7, route 3.7, up 19.9, down 11.0) shows the megakernel is at parity on route and on UP+DOWN (~31 us both) - cross-op overlap is not buying anything yet; both stream experts at only ~1.4 TB/s. Strip probes: per-chunk x reloads from L2 cost ~4.8 us and mma/cvt ~4.2 us; delivery-only still 35 us. Failures: per-group DOWN waits (noise-level), CW=8 (+10 us), CW=2 / >=3 CTAs per SM (+15-60 us), 1 CTA/SM (2x slower), DOWN split even when deterministic (+3-11 us: DOWN tiles queue behind UP tiles). Sweet spot: 264 CTAs x 4 consumer warps x 8-stage ring.
hypothesis: The remaining gap to the 4-launch path is the router GEMV; streaming router weights through the TMA ring as tensor-core tiles (prefetchable before x is ready) closes most of it
title: Megakernel stage 2, round 3: what limits the single-launch MoE block (strip probes, launch-path breakdown, tensor-core router)

conclusion: Small win, still slower: best 40.39 vs 38.44 us/layer (+5%) with L2 evict-first on weight bulk copies (-1 us). ncu: the megakernel reads exactly the weight bytes (199.7 MB / 4 layers, no waste) but sustains only 32% of DRAM peak over the launch (launch-path up/down kernels: 38% / 31%) - both are bound by the serial router -> route -> experts dependency and per-layer ramp/tail, not by bytes. Failures: smem x cache (+14 us: one blocking 20 KB L2 round trip per CTA while L2 queues are full of weight streaming - any L2 round trip on the critical path costs us during streaming), deeper ring (+2 us), 3 CTAs/SM (+7-10 us).
hypothesis: Expert-weight delivery, not compute, bounds the MoE block; removing L2 round trips from consumers and keeping streamed weights out of L2 raises effective bandwidth
title: Megakernel stage 2, round 4: delivery bandwidth of the single-launch MoE block (x cache, ring depth, L2 policy, ncu)

conclusion: Falsified at this design point: 64.42 vs 58.85 us/layer (+9.5%), numerically correct. The timeline confirms cross-op prefetch happens (next layer's dense tiles are claimed and streamed during the MoE DOWN tail), but the gain is smaller than the per-op efficiency lost by running every op through one config (4 consumer warps, 8 x 8 KB ring, 264 CTAs): dense ops take ~22 us here vs 20.1 us as tuned launches, and the MoE stays ~1.5-2 us/layer behind. Prefetch depth is capped by the smem rings (~17 MB grid-wide) and the routing gate still serializes router -> route -> experts.
hypothesis: With dense ops in the same launch, producers fill the MoE's DRAM-idle routing/tail windows with the next layer's dense weights, so one launch beats back-to-back launches
title: Megakernel stage 3 probe: dense GEMVs + MoE block of each layer in ONE persistent launch (weights of the next op prefetch during routing stalls)

conclusion: Falsified. Every prefetch arm is slower than no prefetch (58.5 us/layer): the side-stream fork/join alone costs ~3.4 us/layer (breaks back-to-back launch overlap in the graph), an extra inline launch ~1.9 us, and prefetched bytes cost time roughly in proportion to their size (100% of the next qkvz: +13 us) with no visible L2 hit benefit on the following dense GEMV - even with the MoE's expert loads marked evict_first and the prefetch evict_last. Best net arm (fork, 25%, evict_last) is still +2.4 us. Also verified: SGLang does no weight prefetch on this path - its alt_stream only overlaps in_proj_ba with in_proj_qkvz and the q/k norms; weight-prefetch code exists only for NPU (cmo.py) and DWDP prefill.
hypothesis: DRAM is ~65% idle during the MoE's router/route hops, so cp.async.bulk.prefetch.L2 of the next layer's qkvz/out_proj weights hides their load and shortens the dense GEMVs
title: L2 prefetch of the next layer's dense weights during the MoE (side stream or inline), launch path

conclusion: Wash on both: backoff cap 16-256 ns spans 39.97-40.53 us/layer (noise), and router->route fusion leaves the route end unchanged (11.07 vs 11.2 us) because that hop was only ~0.35 us; the route itself (3.3 us) and router tiles (~5.2 us) dominate. Best megakernel MoE block remains ~40.0 vs ~38.6 us/layer for launches (+4%).
hypothesis: Shorter dependency polling and running ROUTE in the last router tile remove serial hop latency from the per-layer critical path
title: Megakernel stage 2, round 5: polling backoff and router->route fusion in the single-launch MoE block

conclusion: Falsified: the router finishes ~2 us earlier but ROUTE slows by about as much (summing partial logits), net within noise (40.76-41.0 vs 41.47 us/layer in this session's runs). Worse, any K split changes the fp32 summation order before the bf16 rounding of logits and flipped a near-tie expert in one of four layers (routing no longer identical to the reference), so the split is rejected on correctness grounds as well. Default stays RSPLIT=1.
hypothesis: Giving each router warp one chunk instead of two shortens the router tiles on the per-layer critical path
title: Megakernel stage 2, round 6: router K-split (tile = 16 rows x 1/RSPLIT of K, ROUTE sums partial logits in fixed order)

conclusion: Item 3 confirmed, item 2 falsified. CORAL_SPEC_FUSE=1 = 760.5 vs 750.6 tok/s MT-Bench (+1.3%, both rounds), acceptance unchanged (3.24), GSM8K 0.962; the fused kernels are bit-identical to stock (unit-tested incl. argmax ties and dtypes). New best MTP = v27-fuse 760.8 tok/s peak round. Draft-head slicing loses: acceptance drops 3.24 -> 3.12 (16K) / 3.21 (32K), which costs more than the ~0.1 ms/step of draft-head GEMV it saves (709.6 / 737.5 tok/s). Notes: the stock token-map files were id-sorted, so a prefix slice needed a frequency-ranked map (rank49152.pt, same 48K set); rank order alone is neutral within noise (746.1). Profile basis: torch-profiler attribution put ~180 us/step in eager kernels outside CUDA graphs (draft-extend post 26 us, verify commit 24 us, FA3 metadata 22 us, eagle_sample 12 us, overlap stash 10 us, build_tree 8 us). Process issue: the first sequential A/B never ran (its pgrep wait matched itself).
hypothesis: Scoring only the top 16K/32K token-map rows in draft steps 2-4 saves ~0.14 ms/step of draft-head GEMV with little acceptance loss; fusing the eager per-step spec bookkeeping (draft-extend select/gather/argmax, verify commit indices) removes ~17 tiny launches/step from a GPU-bound step
title: MTP draft-phase trims: smaller draft head for draft steps 2-4 (item 2) and fused eager spec-decode bookkeeping (item 3)
